question: How does the Queue (Point-to-Point) pattern differ from Pub/Sub (Topic)?

options.text: Queue delivers the message to all subscribers, Topic — to only one
options.explanation: The opposite. Queue (Point-to-Point) delivers the message to one consumer (first to take it). Topic (Pub/Sub) delivers a copy to every subscriber

options.text: Queue delivers the message to one consumer, Topic — to all subscribers
options.explanation: Queue — load balancing: each message is processed by exactly one consumer. Topic — fanout: every subscriber gets a copy. Queue is for task distribution, Topic is for notifying all interested services

options.text: Queue and Topic are the same thing, just different names in RabbitMQ and Kafka
options.explanation: These are fundamentally different patterns. Queue — one message → one receiver. Topic — one message → all subscribers. Both RabbitMQ and Kafka support both patterns (in Kafka — via consumer groups)

options.text: Queue stores messages, Topic — doesn't
options.explanation: Both store messages. The difference is in delivery semantics: Queue — to one, Topic — to all. In Kafka, both Queue (consumer group) and Topic store messages in a log

question: Which statements about delivery guarantees are correct?

options.text: At-least-once may deliver a message multiple times — therefore idempotency is needed
options.explanation: At-least-once guarantees: the message will definitely be delivered, but may arrive again (if the consumer crashed after processing but before ack). The consumer must be idempotent — repeated processing must not change the result

options.text: Exactly-once is easy to implement between any two services
options.explanation: Exactly-once between services is practically impossible in distributed systems (Two Generals Problem). Kafka implements it only within itself (producer → broker → consumer). As soon as the consumer writes to an external DB — idempotency is needed

options.text: At-most-once is suitable for logs and metrics, where losing individual messages is acceptable
options.explanation: At-most-once — fire-and-forget. Fast, but a message may be lost. Ideal for non-critical data: analytics, logs, metrics. For orders and payments — unacceptable

options.text: At-least-once is the standard guarantee for business logic in production
options.explanation: At-least-once — the gold standard. Message loss is unacceptable for business, and idempotency handles duplicates. Almost all production systems use at-least-once + idempotent consumers

question: What is a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) and why is it needed?

options.text: A queue for messages that couldn't be processed after several attempts
options.explanation: DLQ is a 'quarantine' for problematic messages. After N failed processing attempts (poison messages), the message is moved to the DLQ instead of infinite retry. This prevents blocking the main queue and allows the issue to be resolved manually or automatically

options.text: A queue for deleted messages so they can be restored
options.explanation: DLQ is not a trash bin for deleted messages. It's a queue for messages the consumer couldn't process. They weren't intentionally deleted — a processing error occurred (invalid data, code bug, unavailable external service)

options.text: A temporary queue for messages with expired TTL
options.explanation: TTL is one reason messages end up in the DLQ, but not the only one. The main reason is processing errors. The DLQ accepts messages after exceeding the retry limit or on timeout

options.text: A special queue in Kafka for storing offsets
options.explanation: In Kafka, offsets are stored in a special topic __consumer_offsets, which is not a DLQ. Dead Letter Queue is an error-handling pattern applicable to any broker (RabbitMQ, Kafka, SQS)

question: You have an e-commerce: when an order is created, you need to send an email, update analytics, reserve inventory, and check for fraud. How would you design this?

options.text: HTTP calls to all 4 services synchronously from the Order Service
options.explanation: Order creation will take the sum of all 4 services' latencies. If one service is down — the entire order won't be created. Tight coupling: Order Service must know about all downstream services

options.text: Publish OrderCreated event to a topic, all 4 services subscribe (Pub/Sub)
options.explanation: Pub/Sub is ideal: Order Service publishes one event and doesn't know about subscribers. Each service processes independently. If Email is down — Inventory still works. Easy to add a new service (Loyalty Points) without changing Order Service

options.text: 4 separate queues (Point-to-Point), Order Service puts in each one
options.explanation: It works, but Order Service knows about all queues — tight coupling. When adding a new service (Loyalty), you need to change Order Service. Pub/Sub solves this: one publish → all subscribers receive

options.text: A cron job checks new orders every 5 seconds and dispatches
options.explanation: Polling is an anti-pattern for real-time processing. Up to 5 seconds delay, load on DB from constant queries, difficulty tracking 'already processed' orders. Event-driven (Pub/Sub) reacts instantly

question: Which statements about Kafka are correct?

options.text: Kafka stores messages as an append-only log — you can 'rewind' and re-read
options.explanation: Kafka is a distributed log. Messages aren't deleted after reading, they are stored for a certain time (retention period). A consumer can rewind the offset and re-read all events — useful for data recovery or adding a new service

options.text: In Kafka, the number of consumers in a group can exceed the number of partitions
options.explanation: Each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer in the group. If consumers > partitions, the extra consumers are idle. Rule: partitions >= consumers. For more parallelism — add partitions

options.text: Kafka guarantees message order within a single partition
options.explanation: Within a partition, order is strictly guaranteed (append-only). Between partitions, order is NOT guaranteed. That's why all events for one user are sent to one partition (via key) to preserve order

options.text: Kafka is ideal for simple task queues with small volume
options.explanation: For simple task queues (resize image, send email), RabbitMQ is simpler and more convenient: smart routing, priorities, built-in retry. Kafka is justified for high-load event streaming, logs, analytics, CQRS
